Introduction and Background of Chronotypes

Modern research has defined chronotype as “a biological surrogate for an individual’s phase of entrainment.” In other words, it is a measurable proxy of an individual’s internal clock’s alignment with external factors (Roenneberg, 2012). Chronotypes have extensive impacts in daily life- it affects our preferred bedtime, preferred wakeup time, and even productivity and health.

How did chronotypes come to be? From an evolutionary lens, chronotypes evolved because a tribe would require at least one person awake to keep everyone safe because sleep is a state of vulnerability to predators. This is known as the sentinel hypothesis: group animals have asynchronous sleep times because at least one person would need to stay attentive to the surroundings. Samson et al. (2017) found that 99.8% of tribe members in a hunter-gatherer group were awake between the time the first member went to sleep and the last woke up. This study on a tribe’s sleep pattern shows how modern differences in our chronotypes may be caused by natural selection, working as a group defense mechanism humans evolved to counteract the susceptibility to danger during sleep.

The Biological Mechanism Behind Differences in Chronotypes

The first trace of research regarding chronotypes originated in 1900 when O’Shea published his observations on differences between peak intellectual and physical timings in the book Aspects of Economy. However, chronotypes were only relevantly established as biological mechanisms in 1976 by Horne & Ostbërg. Set out with the aim of revising the concepts of “morningness” and “eveningness”, the two researchers created a 19-question multiple choice questionnaire about sleep preferences. The questionnaire included questions such as “If you went to bed at 11:00 PM at what level of tiredness would you be?” and “When you have no commitments the next day, what time do you go to bed compared to your usual bedtime?”. Each answer had a score assigned that would cumulate to a total, with a lower score indicating an evening preference and higher score indicating a morning preference. After allowing their participants to complete the questionnaire, they were grouped into 3 categories: morning, intermediate, and evening type. The result of the participants’ questionnaires directly correlated with body temperature, validating the science of chronotypes.

[Insert Figure 1 Add-in]

This graph displays a clear biological distinction between morning and evening types. Starting from 9am, the morning types started their day with a higher body temperature and maintained the upper end until about 8pm, where the trendlines for morning and evening types intersected and the temperature dynamic reversed. While the study showed that both morning and evening types both peaked in body temperature during the evening (7:32PM for morning type and 8:40PM for evening type), morning types had higher body temperatures to start the day along with an earlier temperature peak and decline. On the other hand, evening types had lower body temperatures to start the day, but their peak and decline in body temperature was later in the evening (Horne & Ostbërg, 1976). Replications of this experiment have consistently found that morning types have higher body temperatures in the morning and subsequent earlier peaks and declines compared to evening types. Horne and Ostbërg’s research has been instrumental in paving the way for more chronotype research after their paper was published. Their 19-item questionnaire served as a standard for future researchers to use in assigning their own participants into chronotype groups (Baehr et al., 2000; Bailey & Heitkemper, 2001; Duffy et al., 1999; Kerkhof & Van Dongen, 1996). The morning, intermediate, and evening types for chronotypes are still the most relevant categories today.

Chronotypes and Physical Performance

Muscle temperature has direct impacts on performance- for every 1 degree celsius increase in body temperature, performance increase by approximately 3.5% (Wilson et al., 2025). Body temperature means a higher muscle temperature, because blood carries core heat directly to the skeletal tissues. Therefore, the level of baseline body temperatures may have a direct impact on an athlete’s performance (Dykstra, 2024). Chronotypes have been found to differ in onset of body temperature by Horne & Ostberg’s study and its replications. Body temperature may explain the relationship between chronotype and exercise, because chronotype is associated with body temperature timings which could in turn affect exercise. However, research in this field is currently limited and the causation between body temperature and chronotypes cannot be fully established. There may only be speculation that chronotypes have specific differences in time-of-day related physical performance levels.

Chronotypes, Social Jetlag, and Mental Disorders

Social Jetlag is the difference between an individual’s preferred sleep schedule and their actual sleep schedule that is caused by societal factors such as work, school, or family. The most common workday in the U.S starts at 8AM, with only marginal differences in work start times across many other countries such as Japan, China, UK, and Germany (Torpey, 2015). For instance, the most common workday starts at 8:30AM in Japan but 9AM in China.

Chronotypess’ relationship with our work-life schedules are related to mental health outcomes. For example, Zou et al. (2022)’s narrative review has found that evening chronotypes are more likely to have mental disorders, while being a morning type is a protective factor against mental disorders. Moreover, a Dutch correlational study found that the evening chronotype was not only correlated with worse reported mood in the morning, but was also associated with major depressive disorder (Antypa et al., 2015). A plausible explanation for these findings is sleep deprivation. Compared with morning types, both evening and intermediate types have a greater risk for insomnia- evening types are 247% and intermediate types 61% more likely to have insomnia than morning types. Insomnia is the condition of difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or having good quality sleep (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2022). Since evening types have delayed internal rhythms compared to morning types, it is harder for them to adjust to a misaligned sleep schedule—inducing insomnia-like symptoms and increasing the risk of developing insomnia. In brief, evening types are at a greater risk for having physical, mental, and social issues in daily life because of circadian misalignment (a.k.a social jetlag).

Although Patient F’s story does not establish causation between chronotypes and mental illnesses, it is an illustration of how her chronotype affected her response to a schedule change in life. Conclusion

Chronotypes are a measure of how intrinsic rhythms align with environmental factors; it relates to body temperature, responses to schedule changes, physical performance at specific times, and sleep in general. We can all take time to reflect on how our own chronotypes impact how we interact with this world, along with the steps that can be taken to improve it.

Chronotypes’ relation with societal timings raises a broader question: are early start times for work and night shifts benefitting society, or is it degrading individual health? Anyhow, the most important takeaway from this chapter should be that sleep should never be compromised- all chronotype-related issues arise from sleep, so always give yourself a good night’s sleep.

CHAPTER ADD-INS Add in #1

Questionnaire. By using a sextic polynomial model, Horne & Ostbërg fitted a least-squares curve and found the time when every individual’s temperature peaked. Using those fitted curves, they computed a point for every hour from 9AM to 11PM. Each point on the 3 different trendlines corresponds to the average of the all individual graph temperatures for that specific group at that hour. Significant differences were found between the morning type and evening type, while the intermediate type showed no significant differences with either group.

Add in #2

When a 30-year-old woman brought herself to a health clinic, she was displaying symptoms of stress, depression, urge to sleep, and anxiety. At the age of 19, she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder but managed to graduate from university while undergoing treatment. After almost a complete recovery from her mental disorder, she worked morning and afternoon shifts which allowed her to function regularly. However, after switching to night shifts months before she presented herself at the clinic, her life was off balance and was overwhelmed with mental and physical health issues. The clinic diagnosed her as an extreme morning type using the morning-eveningness 19-item questionnaire, and suggested she quit her night shifts to recover a normal life. After 3 days without working night shifts, her mental state improved (Meyrer et al., 2009).

GLOSSARY

TermDefinition
Chronotypesa biological surrogate for an individual’s phase of entrainment
morningnessthose who show extreme preferences for daytime activity; in these individuals, peak performance and alertness is associated with the early-morning hours
eveningnessextreme preferences for nighttime activities; in these individuals, heightened alertness and peak performance is linked to the evening hours
Social Jetlagthe difference between an individual’s preferred sleep schedule and their actual sleep schedule that is caused by societal factors such as work, school, or family
Major depressive disordera common and serious mental health condition defined by a persistent low mood and a loss of interest or pleasure in daily activities

Insomnia

the condition of difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or having good quality sleep
